extracted.intended_audience: academics, researchers, museum curators, students, and general readers interested in Indigenous histories and primary sources
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for treating, using, and interpreting Indigenous oral histories and related primary sources (artifacts, colonial documents) in research, museums, legal contexts, and public history. Emphasizes cultural protocols, decolonizing practice, and critical assessment of documentary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral histories as primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral histories — a type of primary source — let Indigenous peoples teach about their own cultures in their own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use oral histories to transmit important histories, stories and teachings to new generations and to highlight Indigenous perspectives in academic, museum, and public-history work; treat them as firsthand accounts rather than secondary commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and methodological framing of oral history
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral history is defined (by the Oral History Association) as a “method of gathering, preserving and interpreting the voices and memories of people, communities, and participants in past events.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach oral history as an intentional research method involving collection, preservation, and interpretation of memories and voices; recognize it as one of the oldest ways of retelling historical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect cultural custodianship and storytelling protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: In many Indigenous communities, respected individuals (Elders, hereditary chiefs) have responsibility for sharing and maintaining oral histories; some stories can only be told at certain times and places, and by certain people to select audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow community protocols about who may tell a story, when and where it may be told, and to whom; obtain permission and defer to the authority of holders of knowledge (example communities: Mowachaht, Kwakwaka’wakw, Plains communities with winter-only stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize oral histories for audience needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Elders or knowledge-holders may contextualize oral histories depending on the type of message the listening audience needs to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that stories may be framed or adapted for different audiences and purposes; researchers and curators should record and respect contextualizing information provided by narrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize colonial impacts and support reclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Indigenous oral histories have been threatened by colonization; Western privileging of the written word and colonial policies (e.g., the Indian Act, residential schools) forbade the transmission of oral traditions and caused lasting harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the damaging effects of colonization, support Indigenous communities in reclaiming lost or threatened oral traditions, and avoid reproducing colonial assumptions about reliability or value of oral versus written sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use oral histories to decolonize historical narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside Indigenous communities, the use of oral histories serves as a way to decolonize Canadian history by reinserting Indigenous narratives that were historically overlooked or ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include oral histories alongside other evidence to provide first-hand Indigenous accounts; consult and follow recommendations from reports such as the Task Force Report on Museums and First Peoples, the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples, and the TRC’s report to guide inclusive practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat oral histories as valid legal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Canadian courts have recognized oral history as an important type of evidence that must be treated as equal to other types of evidence (notably in Delgamuukw, 1997).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using oral histories in legal or rights-related contexts, respect their evidentiary value and ensure they are presented with appropriate contextualization and attribution; recognize the precedent’s impact on cases about Aboriginal title and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material culture and artifacts as primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Other primary sources—historical clothing, weapons, accessories and artifacts—can transmit Indigenous knowledge and be used to glean historical information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply material culture research methods (examine materials, beadwork, construction, etc.) to identify community of origin and approximate dates; use artifacts to uncover relationships between people and belongings and to supplement oral histories for a fuller picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically evaluate Euro-Canadian documentary sources for bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Euro-Canadian historical documents (records, notebooks, diaries, letters, photographs) may be useful but were often created by colonial government employees or supporters of colonization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always take into account the points of view and positionality of document creators; read such sources critically and situate them alongside Indigenous oral histories and material culture to avoid reproducing colonial perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Museum practices: inclusion and repatriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Museum policies and programs (e.g., the Task Force Report 'Turning the Page') have encouraged inclusion of Indigenous perspectives; some museums have made efforts to return Indigenous artifacts to communities as a means of reconciliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Museums and curators should pursue inclusive policies, consult with Indigenous communities, and consider repatriation of artifacts as part of reconciliation and ethical stewardship of primary sources.
